items.title: Bill Huntington Interview, 1961-12-27
items.q: And then I learned that Lawrence was in town and I started taking from Lawrence. And the arrangement was that Lawrence would come up to the house.

ctx.x: know? Who did you listen to? Who did you remember? You said Bunk Johnson for long, or else?

Let's see. Mostly Bunk. I can't think of anybody else offhand that I really listened to. I listened to Bunk and George and basically those people. Basically the album that Bunk put out, you know, when he went to New York, the Columbia album. And that was very interesting to me. What tunes were on that? High Society. I remember High Society and I remember Snagget. Snagget was on there. And that's all I can recall right now. But I used to listen to that album over and over again. It was very stimulating. And later…
Sure. Yeah, just talk. Just say anything that comes to your mind. No, I'd rather not do that. . .

items.title: Alcide "Slow Drag" Pavageau and Lawrence Marrero Interview, 1957-09-01
items.q: You remember him, Bill Huntington? He was in the store Monday night.

ctx.x: Well this finger is catching all the chords? This one here. All the strings? It's catching except the big, except the C. Yeah. I see. That makes your... See? That'd be kind of good. You make your B front back.

Well I see, I figure the easy way is the best way. I mean for you when you make your own place something you can kill. That's right. The thing that I know of, I don't know everything, but the thing that I do know, I'd be glad to help you out on it. I had a pretty good little band of players. You remember him, Bill Huntington? He was in the store Monday night.
Yeah. When the spotter came by. Well him, Bill Huntington.

items.title: Bill Huntington and Charlie Suhor Interview, 1992-04-06
items.q: your lack of a peer group when you were with Lawrence Marrero and the black musicians

ctx.x: But, I mean, at the time, you would have some of the very greatest jazz musicians, modernists playing in one of the rooms, you know, and that's where I first met Ellis. There's an interesting story that Ellis has related on a television program recently that he did. And I remember this incident, too. I was playing with a pianist by the name of Eddie Finassi, and Ellis hit a trio with Marshall Smith and James Black, and they were playing upstairs in the room upstairs. And, by the way, Al Boleto was an early…

So, before you get too far into your bass stuff, I wanted to pick up on something you said about your lack of a peer group when you were with Lawrence Marrero and the black musicians. That was one thing that I think is very unique about you, the fact that of all the players like myself and others who came up with Dixieland as our love, we just didn't have that deep connection with the early traditional players. And it's easier conceptually to pick up the fluff aspects of Dixieland. It's very difficult, it sounds…
Yeah, well, thanks. You know, I don't really know why it happened except that, to me, the older black players embodied what I wanted to hear.
